explanations.answer: That it is perfect in beauty
explanations.explanation: That's the one. God quotes Tyre's own words: "You have said, O Tyre, ‘I am perfect in beauty.’" (Ezekiel 27:3) Notice the line is Tyre talking about itself. I once spent years in a drawer, and nobody caught me bragging about my looks back there.

explanations.answer: That it can never be conquered
explanations.explanation: Tyre does say something big about itself, but this isn't it. The verse has God quoting Tyre: "I am perfect in beauty." Nothing in these verses has Tyre claiming it can't be conquered. Easy mix-up when a city is described as strong, friend.

explanations.answer: That it is older than every city
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Nothing in the passage has Tyre bragging about its age. What God quotes is "I am perfect in beauty." (Ezekiel 27:3) Looks, not birthdays.

Ship it is! Planking, a mast, and in the next verses oars, a deck and a sail all belong on a vessel. God is describing Tyre like a grand ship, with cypress from Senir and a cedar from Lebanon doing the heavy lifting. Picture the lumber yard that order took.

I see why a builder's list sounds like a temple. But planking and a mast don't go on one. They belong on a ship, and the verses after this one add oars, a deck and a sail. Nobody hoists a sail over an altar.

A tower does need lumber, so good thinking. But a mast is a ship's pole, and this list keeps going with oars, a deck and a sail. The towers show up later in the passage, with men of Gammad standing in them (Ezekiel 27:11). This part of the picture is all ship.

Egypt, right on the money. The sail is made of "…embroidered fine linen from Egypt…" and it serves as the ship's banner (Ezekiel 27:7). So the sail isn't just catching wind, it's showing off. A sail doing double duty, that's a hard-working piece of cloth.
Moab is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't use it. The linen sail comes from Egypt. The blue and purple for the awning come from the coasts of Elishah. Keep your eyes on that sail, friend.

Assyria sounds like it could fit, but it isn't in this verse. The text says the embroidered fine linen for the sail is from Egypt. The awning gets its own source: blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah. Different fabric, different shop.

Right, the captains come from Tyre itself. The verse says, "Your men of skill, O Tyre, were there as your captains." (Ezekiel 27:8) So the oars are pulled by men from Sidon and Arvad, while Tyre's own skilled men steer. Even a ship this grand had a crew from all over.

Persia does show up in this passage, just not at the helm. The men of Persia, Lydia and Put serve as warriors in Tyre's army (Ezekiel 27:10). The captains are Tyre's own men of skill. Right country list, different job.

Egypt is in this passage, but as the source of the linen sail (Ezekiel 27:7). The verse about captains says, "Your men of skill, O Tyre, were there as your captains." So the captains are Tyre's own. Egypt is supplying the cloth, not steering the ship.

True. The elders of Gebal come aboard as shipwrights, "…repairing your leaks." (Ezekiel 27:9) So even a ship called perfect in beauty needs patching. Perfect in beauty, and still calling the repair crew.

The text says the opposite. The elders of Gebal were aboard as shipwrights, "…repairing your leaks." (Ezekiel 27:9) So this ship does have leaks, and it has people on board to fix them. Beautiful, and still in need of a repair crew.

Yes! "All the ships of the sea and their sailors came alongside to barter for your merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:9) They come to trade, not to fight. It's a busy harbor, and Tyre's goods are what bring the ships in. Picture a whole fleet lining up like customers at the bakery door on a holiday morning.

Nothing in the verse says they come to attack. It says they "…came alongside to barter for your merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:9) The walls get their own picture in the next verses, with warriors and hanging shields. Here it's shopping, not a siege.
No rescue in this verse, friend. The ships come alongside "…to barter for your merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:9) They're there for the goods. Sailors are doing business.

True. Of the warriors from Persia, Lydia and Put, the text says, "they gave you splendor." (Ezekiel 27:10) The men on the walls hang their shields around them, and the text says "they perfected your beauty." (Ezekiel 27:11) Even the armor is part of the decorating.

The text says it does. The warriors hang their shields and helmets on Tyre's walls, and "they gave you splendor." (Ezekiel 27:10) The shields hung around the walls "…perfected your beauty." (Ezekiel 27:11) So all that hardware counts as decoration here.

That's it. "Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea." (Ezekiel 27:26) God names the east wind. The oarsmen got the ship way out there, and the wind is what shatters it. It's a sudden turn after a very big, busy picture.
No fire in this verse. God says, "…the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea." (Ezekiel 27:26) The text keeps the whole scene on the water. Wind, not flames.

No fish in this verse, friend. The text says "…the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea." (Ezekiel 27:26) The oarsmen have brought the ship out onto the high seas, and the east wind is what shatters it. Wind is the one God names.

True. Tyre's wealth, wares and merchandise, its sailors, captains and shipwrights, its merchants and all the warriors will "…sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall." (Ezekiel 27:27) The list is long, the same way the building of the ship was. I think that's a heavy verse, and it's worth sitting with.

The text says it does happen. Tyre's wealth, wares and merchandise, its sailors, captains and shipwrights, its merchants and all the warriors within it "…will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall." (Ezekiel 27:27) So it's the people and the goods going down together. I think this is one of the heavy parts.

Shore, yes. "All who handle the oars will abandon their ships. The sailors and all the captains of the sea will stand on the shore." (Ezekiel 27:29) First they leave their ships, then they stand on the shore. The ones who ran the sea end up standing on land. That's a big change of scenery.

Hills are a fair guess for a place to stand and watch. But the text puts them elsewhere: "The sailors and all the captains of the sea will stand on the shore." (Ezekiel 27:29) They've left their ships and are standing at the water's edge. Close to the sea, even without a boat.

The sailors aren't on the decks in this picture. The verse says the oarsmen "…will abandon their ships." and then the sailors and captains "…will stand on the shore." (Ezekiel 27:29) They leave the ships and end up on the shore. The decks are not where the verse puts them.
Yes. The text says, "They will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning." (Ezekiel 27:31) Dust on heads, ashes and sackcloth all go with that grief. I think this one is heavy.

The verse doesn't show anger. It says the sailors "…will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning." (Ezekiel 27:31) The dust, the ashes and the sackcloth go with that weeping. They're grieving over Tyre.

The text doesn't say that here. It says the sailors "…will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning." (Ezekiel 27:31) The mourning is over Tyre. Nothing in the verse says it's about their own sins.

Enriched, that's the word. The sailors say, "You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:33) They also say, "…you satisfied many nations." The lament remembers what Tyre's trade gave to others.

Ruined would be a sour way to remember it. In the lament the sailors say, "You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:33) So they look back at what Tyre's wares did for kings. No ruin in that line.

Ignored isn't it, friend. The lament says, "You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:33) Tyre's goods went out to sea and reached many nations. That's the opposite of ignoring.
Right. In the lament, "All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you." (Ezekiel 27:35) The kings shudder with fear and their faces are contorted. It's shock all around the coast.

No cheering in this verse. The lament says, "All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you. Their kings shudder with fear; their faces are contorted." (Ezekiel 27:35) It's a shocked, fearful scene. Not a party.

Nobody rushes in with hammers here. The lament says, "All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you." (Ezekiel 27:35) The kings shudder with fear. Appalled is what the verse gives, not rebuilding.

The lament doesn't end that way. Its last line says, "you have come to a horrible end and will be no more." (Ezekiel 27:36) So there's no hope of rising again in these words. It's a heavy ending, and I think it hurts to read.

False is right, and I'm sorry it's such a heavy one. The lament closes with, "you have come to a horrible end and will be no more." (Ezekiel 27:36) Those who trade among the nations hiss at Tyre, and no rising again is mentioned. That's where the sailors' lament stops.
